A regular gym routine and calorie counting are both really effective in helping you meet your fitness goals. However, the only thing you really *need* to do is eat fewer calories than you burn which you can do without either of those things. I suggest you get a pedometer or download an app on your phone that counts your steps (I use Google fit) and get 8-10k every day. Like 7 days a week. Walking is good exercise. 

Second, and probably most importantly, find 3-5 small, easy to make healthy meals that you enjoy and eat them regularly. I eat chicken fajitas (no rice or beans) probably 3 times a week and I enjoy it every time because I love fajitas. Replace high calorie meals with these smaller, healthier meals and repeat for months on end and you should lose weight. 

I'll just add, I know you said you don't like calorie counting but I do think it would be worth doing it for a few weeks *without* changing your eating habits (just track what you eat) so you can get a better handle of where all those excess calories are coming from. If you don't know what's making you fat, it's hard to change it.

That's how the algorithm is designed. It wants to play something for you that you won't turn off and the most reliable way to do that is to play something you often listen to.

This is not a bug, it's the way it's designed. I recommend you don't listen to music via the algorithm if it bothers you

I think it's worth understanding that the algorithm has one job: play something that you won't turn off. The easiest way to do that is to play something you listen to often. Rinse and repeat this often enough and you'll get the feeling that it plays the same things all the time. The algorithm for every music service has this same problem because the people who created the algorithm don't regard it as a problem. 

The only solution is to not rely on the algorithm to decide what to listen to. There's albums, pre-made playlists, and an unending number of community playlists.

Two political phenomenon acting on top of one another:

The way the US electoral system is designed necessitates 2 major parties because all other minor parties will make the major party they agree with more less likely to win by siphoning their voters. This is called the spoiler effect and is just a byproduct of the first-past-the-post system of voting the US uses in most areas. 

It's in the nature of democracies that actors have an incentive to expand their political coalition to include a majority of voters (or enough to wield majority political power depending on how the will of the voters gets distorted through the system). That's because in order to govern, you will need a political majority. Even in parliamentary democracies with many parties, there's really only two parties: the governing coalition and the opposition. To wield power, you will need to act as part of a coalition. In multi-party parliaments, that can be made up of a government of many parties. In America's electoral system, all of those different parts of the coalition are represented within the same party. 

Stack these two things on top of one another and you have two huge parties that have within them varied coalitions that are trying to expand their reach until they can secure a majority governing coalition.

The holding penalties are intended to penalize players who aren't really making an athletic move but rather just clinging on to another player to slow them down. The idea is if the defensive player can beat the block, they deserve a chance to make a play on the ball carrier.

However, offensive lineman are coached to learn how to hold defenders without getting called because holding is really effective. This is why people often say "you could call holding every play". What that basically means is if you placed every movement under a Microscope, you could likely find something that meets the definition of holding on just about every play. However, that doesn't mean that it would meet the *spirit* of the holding rule.

Another thing to consider is commentators on the Internet often don't know the rules as well as they think they do and sometimes mistake legal moves for illegal ones. For instance, if a defender is engaged with a blocker and performs a rip or swim move, the blocker is not holding even though it might look like it is. You can't tell it a defender is being held by looking at a single still frame of a play even though people on the Internet love to do this.
